Patient Vignette: Chaplain, Age 44

She still wears the black suit from that day. Not every day, but often. It’s well-pressed, the only one that survived the dry cleaning without a faint, sour smell she can’t quite place. She tells herself it’s practical—a chaplain needs to look professional for hospital visits. But the truth is, it feels like armor.

The event happened eighteen months ago, on a Tuesday. She was at the civic center, serving on a city-wide crisis response team after a mass shooting at a downtown office building. Her role was to stand in the family reunification area, a cavernous room with folding chairs and bad fluorescent lighting. She remembers the hum of the generator, the way the air tasted like dust and adrenaline. She remembers holding the hand of an elderly woman whose daughter-in-law was unaccounted for. The woman’s fingers were cold, and she kept whispering, “She’s just in a meeting. She’s always in a meeting.”

Then the second wave of gunfire came.

It was not supposed to happen. The scene was supposed to be secure. But a secondary attacker had been hiding in a janitorial closet. The sound was not like movies—it was wet, percussive, and impossibly close. She remembers the concrete floor against her cheek, the weight of two other bodies pressing her down. A man’s elbow was digging into her ribs. Someone was crying, a high, thin sound like a wounded animal. She tried to pray, but the words wouldn’t come. All she could think was, This is where I die. This is where I die with my mouth full of dust.

She did not die. But something in her did.

Now, she lives in a small apartment with blackout curtains she never opens. She works the night shift at a suburban hospice, a quiet posting she requested. The daytime is too loud. Too many footsteps. Too many doors closing. She finds herself scanning every room she enters for exits, for hiding places. She cannot sit with her back to a door. At a coffee shop last week, a teenager dropped a tray of ceramic mugs, and she was under the table before she knew she’d moved. The teenager stared. She apologized, her face hot, and left without her coffee.

Her work, once her vocation, has become a series of landmines. She used to pray with families in the ICU waiting room. Now, she avoids it. The fluorescent lights are the same. The smell of antiseptic and grief is the same. Last month, a code blue was called, and the overhead speaker crackled to life. She felt her chest seize, her vision narrowing to a dark tunnel. She excused herself to the chapel and spent forty minutes with her head between her knees, trying to convince herself she was safe.

She has not told her supervisor. She is afraid they will take her off duty. She is afraid they will think she is broken. She is afraid they are right.

At night, she does not sleep. She lies awake and replays it. The elbow in her ribs. The dust. The woman’s cold fingers. Sometimes she hears the wet sound of the gunfire, and she jolts upright, her heart slamming. She has stopped answering her phone. Friends have stopped calling. She eats because she has to, but food tastes like cardboard.

She knows the PCL-5 score is 79. The VA psychologist told her, his voice gentle. She nodded, signed the release form, and walked out into the parking lot, where a car backfired. She spent the next hour in her car, curled in the driver’s seat, her hands over her ears.

She is a chaplain. She is supposed to hold space for suffering. But she has no space left for her own. She carries the dust in her lungs, and every breath tastes like that Tuesday.
